title: TraCE: Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding
claim: Prior explanations leave the motion source ambiguous or incomplete; ours shows what every entity is doing, so users can see the evidence.
layout: Input and model at left, three explanation types on top with matching user reactions below
description: On the left, an input soccer-penalty video (stacked frames) feeds a robot-icon Model. The model outputs the prediction "Soccer Penalty", and an "Explain" arrow points right. A rounded box at the top right holds three explanation types on the same scene. The first is a concept-based heatmap, a rainbow overlay labelled "Concept: Soccer goal". The second is a pose-based concept, a stick-figure skeleton sequence over a time axis. The third is the trajectory-based concept (Ours), with colored chevron arrows on the goalkeeper, the ball and the other player. Below, three speech bubbles show cropped circles of those entities. Each circle has a marker: yellow question marks (a), red crosses (b), green checks (c). A cartoon user appears in each bubble with a quote. The bottom labels are color-coded: (a) Source-ambiguous in yellow, (b) Source-incomplete in red, (c) Source-flexible in green.
caption: Trajectory concepts make motion sources flexible. Existing video XAI often underspecifies which motion source supports a prediction. (a) Heatmap-based explanations [7] can conflate actor motion, object motion, and static context (source-ambiguous). (b) Pose-based concepts [26] cover one person’s joints but omit object motion and interactions (source-incomplete). (c) In contrast, TraCE provides source-flexible motion explanations by representing dynamic evidence from people, objects, and interactions as trajectory concepts.
abstract: Video understanding models often rely on motion, yet their explanations can obscure which motion sources support a prediction. We identify motion-source under-specification as a limitation of existing video XAI: region-centric explanations can be source-ambiguous, while motion vocabularies restricted to single-person pose sequences are source-incomplete. We propose TraCE (Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding), a concept-based framework that discovers source-flexible motion concepts by clustering optical-flow trajectories from training videos. These concepts represent dynamic evidence from people, objects, and interactions, while object and scene concepts account for static context. The resulting typed trajectory/object/scene interface supports class prediction for action recognition and question-conditioned concept matching for video question answering (VQA). We evaluate TraCE across five random seeds on six benchmarks: NTU RGB+D Mutual, Chiral SSv2, UCF-101, KTH, TOMATO, and STAR. Relative to non-interpretable baselines, TraCE maintains competitive task performance, with an average accuracy drop of 1.0 points for action recognition and a nominal gain of 0.4 points for VQA. Motion perturbation and concept-removal tests provide complementary evidence of directional semantic alignment and decision faithfulness, while sample-level interventions illustrate targeted model debugging. Our project page is available at https://leewooil.github.io/TraCE_project_page/.
